turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that is such a tough spot. First off, take a deep breath. Planning this since you were fifteen means this wedding is your baby too, so it makes total sense that you're feeling the weight of it all. 

But running a sangeet *and* doing a high-energy opening dance while fasting is a massive physical ask. It’s completely valid that you're dreading the toll it'll take on your body. You shouldn't have to feel guilty for needing to protect your health and energy during Ramzan.

Have you been totally honest with Shreya about your physical limits for that day? She’s your best friend; she’d probably rather have you present and safe than pushing yourself to the point of passing out. Maybe you could compromise on the dance—something more low-key, emotional, or even partially seated? And please, hand off the "co-director" clipboard to someone else for that specific night so you aren't running around stressing over logistics on an empty stomach. 

How do you think she’d react if you told her you absolutely want to dance with her, but need to tweak the choreography so you don't run out of breath before Iftar?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Ugh, being the rope in a tug-of-war is the most exhausting place to be, especially when both sides are pulling out of love. 

Shreya’s comment is so sweet, but it totally misses the point. She sees it as just skipping a meal, but you and I know it’s a spiritual commitment and a discipline. You can't just "skip one day" without it feeling like you're compromising something deeply personal to you. 

And Ammi’s reaction makes total sense too. For her, Ramzan is about reflection, peace, and ibadat. A loud, glamorous sangeet feels completely out of place to her. It’s a classic clash of worlds and generations.

Here’s the hard part: you might not be able to make them understand perfectly, so you have to advocate for *yourself*. 

With Shreya, maybe shift the conversation. Tell her, "Fasting is a spiritual discipline for me, not just a physical one, so breaking it isn't an option. But I love you, and I want to find a way to celebrate with you that respects both my faith and our friendship." 

With Ammi, maybe reassure her that you deeply respect the sanctity of the month, and you're just going to be there to support your best friend, not to party hard. 

If you take both their voices out of your head for a second... what do *you* actually want to do? Not what Shreya wants, not what Ammi wants, but what feels right in your heart?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

Oh, I completely get why that escape hatch looks so incredibly shiny right now. When you’re this burnt out, a "clean lie" feels like a survival tactic, not a betrayal. You just want the pressure to stop. 

But since you asked me to be real with you... I can't tell you it's not terrible. Not because you're a bad person, but because of the hangover it'll leave you with. 

You guys have been planning this since you were fifteen. If you skip it, you are going to carry the guilt of missing your best friend's wedding for the rest of your life. And Indian weddings have a 100% success rate of accidental exposures—some random auntie will post a story, or someone will mention your "deployment," and Shreya will find out. The heartbreak of her realizing you lied to avoid her will hurt her way more than you saying, "I need to protect my fast."

You’re exhausted because you’re trying to be the perfect co-director, the perfect fasting Muslim, and the perfect daughter all at once. 

What if the "escape" isn't a lie, but just dropping the clipboard? Tell Shreya you love her, but you need to officially step down as co-director for the sangeet so you can just be her best friend that night. You don't have to manage the vendors, you don't have to do the high-energy dance, and you definitely don't have to explain yourself to every auntie. (A simple smile and "I'm fasting, but I'm so happy to be here" works wonders to shut them up).

If you take the logistics off your plate, does being there just as a supportive, fasting friend feel a little more doable?

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

Oh, my heart. That "small stone" and the idea of the "two albums" is such a beautiful, heartbreaking way to put it. It perfectly captures why this feels so impossibly heavy. You feel like you’re holding two fragile, priceless things, and if you move the wrong way, one of them shatters. 

But I want to gently challenge the idea that either of them is that fragile. 

Your *deen* isn't going to break because you're sitting in a beautifully decorated room watching your best friend get married. And Shreya’s *shaadi* isn't going to be ruined if her best friend isn't doing a high-energy Bollywood routine, but is instead sitting in the front row, fasting, and looking at her with so much love. 

You won't be a sad story in either album. In her wedding album, you’ll be the best friend of 18 years who showed up exactly as she is—honoring her faith while celebrating her girl. And in the "album" of your Ramzan, it will be a memory of patience, love, and balancing your devotion to your Creator with your devotion to the people He placed in your life. That’s not a dent. That’s a beautiful, complex, real life.

What if you stopped talking to Shreya about the *logistics* (the dance, the food, the timing) and just told her about the *stone*? What if you said, "Shreya, I love you so much, but I am terrified of getting this wrong. I feel like I'm choosing between my faith and you, and it's breaking my heart." 

She’s your best friend. If she hears the fear in your heart, rather than just a scheduling conflict, I truly believe she’ll drop the clipboard and the choreography and just hold you. How does it feel to imagine saying that to her?
